items.title: The phases of a public service
items.source: GOV.UK Service Manual and Service Standard
items.body: Government services are built in phases. Discovery finds out who the users are and what problem needs solving; the team builds nothing yet and ends with a decision on whether to continue. Alpha tests different ways of solving the problem with prototypes and real users. Beta builds the service for real and tests it, first with a limited group (private beta) and then with anyone (public beta). Live is the running service, which is continually improved. Retirement is the planned end. Each phase has an exit decision based on evidence. Skipping discovery and starting to build from a fixed specification is the most common way for a service to solve the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: Which list shows the phases of a government digital service in order?
What is the main purpose of discovery?

options.text: To build the first working service
To learn about users and the problem before deciding what to build
The team tests different approaches with prototypes and real users

questions.prompt: A programme wants to skip discovery and start building from a detailed specification written two years ago. What risks do you raise?
questions.answer: Needs and technology may have changed, so the service may solve the wrong problem. Without user research the team has little evidence, building is costly to undo and the exit decision from discovery is lost. Recommend a short discovery to test the specification with users and confirm what to build.
questions.rubric: Should point to risk of solving the wrong problem, outdated assumptions, cost of rework, and lack of evidence; and recommend at least a short discovery with user research.

items.title: The Service Standard
items.source: GOV.UK Service Manual and Service Standard
items.body: The Service Standard is a set of 14 points that teams building government services are expected to meet. The first is to understand users and their needs. Others include solving a whole problem for users, providing a joined-up experience across channels, making the service simple to use, making sure everyone can use it (including disabled people and people who are not online), having a multidisciplinary team, using agile ways of working, iterating and improving frequently, keeping the service secure and private, defining what success looks like and publishing performance data, and choosing the right tools and technology. A service assessment is a review by an independent panel at the end of a phase against the Standard, based on evidence from the team. Its job is to help the team improve, not to catch them out.

questions.prompt: How many points are there in the Service Standard?
Which point of the Service Standard comes first?
Which point makes sure disabled people and people who are not online can use a service?

options.text: Make sure everyone can use the service

questions.prompt: What is a service assessment, and how should a team prepare for one?
questions.answer: An independent panel reviews the team's evidence against the Service Standard at the end of a phase, such as alpha or beta, and recommends whether the service should move on. A team prepares by gathering real evidence (research, testing, performance data, plans), being honest about what is not yet met and planning how to fix it, and involving the whole team in the discussion.
questions.rubric: Must say: independent panel, review against the Service Standard at the end of a phase, decides whether to proceed with recommendations. Preparation: evidence from users and testing, honesty about gaps, whole team.

items.title: Beta, go-live and operations
items.source: GOV.UK Service Manual and Service Standard
items.body: In a private beta the service is open to a limited number of invited users, so the team can find problems before they affect everyone. A public beta is open to all. Before going live, the team confirms that support is in place, monitoring and incident routes are ready, there is a way to roll back, performance measures are being collected, the service is accessible and security tests are complete. Going live does not end the team's work: a live service is continually improved, supported and measured, and the service owner remains accountable for it. If a firm launch date collides with unfinished work, such as a failed accessibility test, the team states the risks openly, limits the impact and escalates the decision to the service owner.

options.text: A test done only by the development team
The service is tested with a limited number of invited users
A beta that has no real users

questions.prompt: Which of these is needed before a service goes live?

options.text: A press launch has been booked
Support and incident routes, monitoring and a way to roll back

questions.prompt: What should happen after a service goes live?

options.text: It is supported, measured and continually improved

questions.prompt: A minister's launch date is two weeks away, but testing shows some users who rely on screen readers cannot complete the service. What do you do?
questions.answer: State the risk and impact openly to the service owner and sponsor. Fix the blocking issues if possible, otherwise provide another route for affected users, publish an accurate accessibility statement and plan fixes. Consider a limited launch. The decision is recorded and escalated; it is not hidden or delayed without telling those who decide.
questions.rubric: Should include transparency about the risk, escalation to service owner/sponsor, fix or alternative route, accessibility statement, possibly limited launch, and record of decision. Must not hide the issue.

items.title: Ownership, handover and retirement
items.source: GOV.UK Service Manual and Service Standard
items.body: Each service has a service owner who is accountable for it from end to end, whatever team or supplier does the work. Services end for many reasons: the policy ends, a new service replaces it, use falls away or it costs more than it is worth. A retirement plan tells users what is happening and where to go instead, moves what must be moved, archives what must be kept, switches off systems and ends contracts. When a service is handed to another team or department, a handover pack gives them what they need: how it works, who supports it, the live risks, the contracts, the data held and the open issues. Planning the end early makes it cheaper and safer.

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for a government service from end to end?
Which of these should a retirement plan include?

options.text: Keeping the service running with no owner
Telling users what is happening, archiving data and ending contracts and systems

questions.prompt: What belongs in a handover pack?

options.text: How the service works, who supports it, risks, contracts, data held and open issues

questions.prompt: A service is being transferred to another department. How do you make the handover safe?
questions.answer: Agree who owns what and when, prepare a handover pack with documentation, contacts, support arrangements, risks, contracts, data and open issues, run a period of joint working, transfer access and contracts in a controlled way and confirm in writing that the new owner accepts the service.
questions.rubric: Should include agreed ownership/dates, a handover pack contents, joint-working period, controlled transfer of access/contracts, and formal acceptance.
